questions.stem: Which part of the flower produces pollen grains?
questions.explanation: The anther is the part of the stamen (male part of the flower) that produces pollen grains. Each pollen grain contains the male gamete. The anther is supported by the filament.

questions.stem: What is the female reproductive part of a flower called?
questions.explanation: The carpel (also called the pistil) is the female reproductive part of a flower. It consists of the stigma (which receives pollen), the style, and the ovary (which contains ovules with egg cells).

questions.stem: Where are the egg cells (ovules) found in a flower?
questions.explanation: Egg cells are contained within ovules, which are found inside the ovary at the base of the carpel. After fertilisation, the ovule develops into a seed and the ovary develops into a fruit.

questions.stem: What is the function of petals in insect-pollinated flowers?

options.text: To attract insects with bright colours and scent

questions.explanation: In insect-pollinated flowers, petals are typically large, brightly coloured, and scented to attract insect pollinators. Some also have nectar guides (patterns visible to insects) that direct them towards the nectaries.

questions.stem: What is the function of the stigma?

options.text: To receive and trap pollen grains

questions.explanation: The stigma is the sticky tip of the carpel that receives pollen grains during pollination. In insect-pollinated flowers it is sticky; in wind-pollinated flowers it is feathery to catch pollen from the air.

questions.stem: How do wind-pollinated flowers differ from insect-pollinated flowers?

options.text: Wind-pollinated flowers have large, colourful petals
Wind-pollinated flowers have feathery stigmas and produce lots of light pollen
Wind-pollinated flowers produce large, sticky pollen

questions.explanation: Wind-pollinated flowers have feathery stigmas that hang outside the flower to catch pollen from the air. They produce large quantities of small, light, smooth pollen. They have small or no petals and no scent or nectar.

options.text: Green leaf-like structures that protect the flower bud
The coloured parts that attract pollinators
The tubes that carry pollen to the ovule

questions.explanation: Sepals are the green, leaf-like structures found on the outside of the flower. They protect the developing flower bud before it opens. Together, the sepals form the calyx.
